title: ROSETTA: Constructing Code-Based Reward from Unconstrained Language Preference
claim: A three-stage module turns unconstrained language preferences into reward code that yields diverse behaviors across short- and long-horizon tasks.
layout: 3 columns, left-to-right: preferences, puzzle-piece modules, code, rollout frames; task sidebar
description: The figure reads left to right. At the far left, three user avatars each give a natural-language preference, such as "Way too fast. Let's slow it down.", "Maybe it could just rotate the ball?", and "Move to the right, one target's width". Blue arrows send these preferences into three orange puzzle-piece modules labeled Preference Grounding, Staging and Coding, under the ROSETTA title. Purple arrows lead from the modules to three lavender boxes of generated Python-like reward code. Each code box points to a row of four simulation frames, at t=5 to t=50, showing a robot arm pushing a ball toward a red target. White arrows mark the speed, rotation and shift behaviors. The top row shows the original task. A right-hand sidebar lists example preferences for short-horizon and long-horizon tasks, with small environment images in green and purple panels.
caption: ROSETTA’s three-module structure takes unconstrained, unseen natural language preference and generates reward code that incentivizes desired behavior. ROSETTA can adapt to diverse behavioral preferences, not only in position but orientation and speed. We validate ROSETTA’s performance in two short-horizon and three long-horizon task-agnostic environments.
abstract: Intelligent embodied agents not only need to accomplish preset tasks, but also learn to align with individual human needs and preferences. Extracting reward signals from human language preferences allows an embodied agent to adapt through reinforcement learning. However, human language preferences are unconstrained, diverse, and dynamic, making constructing learnable reward from them a major challenge. We present ROSETTA, a framework that uses foundation models to ground and disambiguate unconstrained natural language preference, construct multi-stage reward functions, and implement them with code generation. Unlike prior works requiring extensive offline training to get general reward models or fine-grained correction on a single task, ROSETTA allows agents to adapt online to preference that evolves and is diverse in language and content. We test ROSETTA on both short-horizon and long-horizon manipulation tasks and conduct extensive human evaluation, finding that ROSETTA outperforms SOTA baselines and achieves 87% average success rate and 86% human satisfaction across 116 preferences.
